title: A name that stores an accent apart from its letter, as macOS writes names, isn't found by typing the letter
problem: Found by the reviewer of 'typo-fallback-near-miss' (done record: /home/user/polish-tools/done/typo-fallback-near-miss.json, second item under 'Found, not fixed', and the review fix `may_be_spelled_apart`). A letter with an accent can be stored as one character (`é`, U+00E9) or as two (`e` and a combining accent, U+0065 U+0301). A keyboard types the one; names made in Finder and most Mac apps store the two. The search compares names as stored, character by character. So a name whose accents are stored apart never has a typed `é` (or `å`, `ö`, `ü`, `ñ`) in order: `is_subsequence("señor", "sen\u{303}or.txt")` is false. Such a name is found only through the typo fallback, which the review of 'typo-fallback-near-miss' deliberately kept loose for it (`may_be_spelled_apart`: where the word and the path both have a letter beyond ASCII, fff-search's match stands): the file is listed among fff-search's far misses, without highlight; it is not found at all with Allow typos off, or when the word is quoted; an app with such a name is not found; and a typo in a word typed without accents costs one typo more for every accent mark inside the run it is compared with (`bjrok` against a Björk stored apart finds nothing). The other way round, a word typed without accents against a name that has them as one character counts a wrong letter for each: `senor` finds `señor.txt`, `resume` does not find `Résumé.pdf` (two in six letters). For anyone whose files have such letters in their names, on a Mac, searching by name is unreliable.
proposal: Reproduce first with engine tests: files whose names store accents apart can be made on Linux (a name is bytes there; engine::tests::a_name_that_stores_an_accent_apart_is_found_by_the_letter_typed writes two), searched for with the composed letter, with Allow typos on and off, quoted and unquoted. Then make the comparison blind to how a letter is stored. Two halves. (1) What fff-search is asked: its matching is by character, so a query typed composed does not match a name stored apart except as a typo. When a query's composed and decomposed forms differ, the engine can ask for both and merge the answers by path, as it already merges two searches for a query with capitals and a file search with a folder search ('fuzzy-word-case' and 'result-tie-break' describe how those merges keep the order and the cut). (2) The engine's own checks, which decide what is kept, ranked and highlighted: `is_subsequence`, `near_miss`, the quoted-phrase check (`contains_phrase`), `rerank` and `spells`, the app names in `app_hits`, `strict_words` for `changes_for`, and the highlight needle. Normalize the words and the text they are compared with to one form at the places they are made (`hit.rel`, the display name, the words), so that every check sees the same spelling, and take `may_be_spelled_apart` out once names are found without it. Highlight ranges are positions in the name as it is shown, so a normalized copy must map back to the stored name's positions, or the highlight must be computed on the stored name with a comparison that is blind to the form; say which you did and test a highlighted row. For the normalizing itself prefer a crate that is already in Cargo.lock over a new one (`icu_normalizer` is there through other crates; check `cargo tree -i icu_normalizer` and what a direct dependency on it costs in build time and binary size); `unicode-normalization` is the usual small crate if that is unreasonable. Whichever you add, say so prominently in the commit message and your notes: a new dependency is the owner's call. Optional, only if it falls out of the same work and stays small: a word typed without accents finds a name that has them (`resume` finds `Résumé.pdf`), as Finder's search does, by also comparing with the accents taken off; if you do it, an exact-accent match must still rank first.
original_test_plan: Engine tests that fail today, on files whose names store accents apart and files that store them as one character: each is found by the word typed composed, first or among the real matches, with Allow typos off as well as on; a quoted word finds it; the row's highlight covers the word; a typo in such a word is still a near miss within its budget; an app with such a name is found (see engine::tests::finds_apps_without_indexing_them for how apps are staged). Guards: ASCII searches list exactly what they list today (compare whole lists for a set of searches), and cost the same; a name with letters from another script (Cyrillic, Greek, CJK) is found by its own letters. If you add accent-blind matching: `resume` finds `Résumé.pdf`, and `résumé` ranks the accented name ahead of `resume.pdf`.
original_risks: The search path every keystroke runs. Normalizing every candidate's path on every search costs time: measure a one-letter search of a large tree before and after, and normalize lazily (only when the query or the text is not ASCII) if it shows. Asking fff-search twice doubles that part of a search for queries with accents only; say what it costs. Byte offsets: anything that slices a name by positions found in a normalized copy will cut inside a character and panic; the highlight is where that can happen. The pool fff-search returns is cut before the engine's checks ('result-tie-break'): a merged pool must keep its order and its cut honest (`truncated`, the `+` in the count). macOS and Windows cannot be run here: APFS keeps a name as it is given, by what the earlier reviewer knew and not by a run; write the tests so that they accept the name in either spelling back from the disk, as the existing test does.

verifier.claim_check: Not checked by a second reviewer. The reviewer of 'typo-fallback-near-miss' built a fixture of 22 names with accents stored apart and ran 21 searches typed with composed letters against the trunk, the implementer's commit and the final code; their record has the numbers. That macOS stores names this way is from their knowledge and the orchestrator's, not from a run. Reproduce the search half on Linux before changing anything.
verifier.implementation_notes: See the proposal: a starting point, not a checked plan. Read the done records of 'typo-fallback-near-miss', 'fuzzy-word-case' and 'result-tie-break' first.

orchestrator_notes: 'near-miss-beside-scattered' (queued) changes when near misses are kept, in the same function; whichever of the two lands second rebases over the other. The manual's Allow typos row has a sentence about words with an accent or in another alphabet being held to the near-miss rule only on paths that are all in A to Z: that sentence describes `may_be_spelled_apart` and goes when the function goes.
